31544: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, grew up in Rome among the imperial family and through friendship with Caligula and Claudius came to rule all the territory his grandfather had held (37-44). Popular with Jewish crowds for his observance, he executed James son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter. Acts and Josephus independently describe his sudden death at Caesarea after he accepted acclaim as a god.
31545: Acts 12 calls him King Herod, says he killed James with the sword, arrested Peter to please the Jews, and died after being struck by an angel of the Lord for accepting divine honors.
31546: His death is read as divine judgment on a persecutor and on human pride, contrasted with the word of God continuing to grow (Acts 12:24).
31547: Josephus's account closely parallels Acts: games at Caesarea in honor of Caesar, a robe of silver shining in the sun, flatterers hailing him as a god, sudden abdominal pain and death five days later. Some suggest a medical cause such as poisoning or intestinal obstruction; the agreement is often cited as evidence for Luke's accuracy.
31548: Remembered favorably in the Mishnah (Sotah 7:8), which describes him weeping while reading Deuteronomy at the festival and the people reassuring him that he was their brother.
31549: At Caesarea, in a garment woven of silver, he was hailed as a god; he did not rebuke them, saw an owl as an omen, was seized with violent pains, and died after five days.
31551: Charming, ambitious and image-conscious; a courtier raised in Rome who speaks the language of piety to the crowd and of patronage to the powerful.
31553: Third year of Trajan per Photius citing Justus of Tiberias
31556: client king of territories north and east of Galilee
31557: overseer of the temple and high-priestly appointments
31558: Expert in Jewish customs and controversies
31560: Agrippa and his sister Bernice come to welcome the new governor; Festus lays Paul's case before him, and Agrippa asks to hear Paul.
31562: With great pomp Agrippa hears Paul tell of his conversion. Paul asks whether he believes the prophets; Agrippa replies, in words translated either almost you persuade me or in so short a time would you persuade me to be a Christian?
31564: Agrippa tells Festus that Paul could have been released had he not appealed to Caesar.
31565: Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I, was the last ruler of the Herodian line. Too young to inherit his father's kingdom in 44, he later ruled territories in the north under Rome and held the right to appoint high priests. With his sister Bernice he heard Paul's defense at Caesarea and judged him innocent of any capital offense. During the Jewish revolt he sided with Rome and lived on as a client king into the 90s.
31566: Acts presents Agrippa as well versed in Jewish customs; Paul appeals to his belief in the prophets, and Agrippa responds with an ambiguous question about being persuaded to become a Christian, then declares Paul innocent.
31567: Agrippa's reply (KJV: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian) became a classic text on the danger of being nearly persuaded; most modern translations read it as skeptical or ironic.
31568: Josephus records Agrippa's attempt to dissuade Jerusalem from revolt in 66 (War 2.345-404, a speech composed by Josephus) and his deposition of the high priest Ananus after James's execution (Antiquities 20.203).
31569: Rumors circulated of an incestuous relationship between Agrippa and his sister Bernice.
31571: Urbane, curious and noncommittal; enjoys a good argument about Jewish law but keeps one eye on Rome.
31576: Early recall date argued by some
31582: Claudius Lysias sends Paul to Felix with a letter; Felix holds him in Herod's praetorium pending his accusers' arrival.
31583: Hears the case and postpones it
31584: After the orator Tertullus accuses Paul and Paul answers, Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, adjourns the case and gives Paul some liberty.
31585: Alarmed by Paul's preaching; hopes for a bribe
31586: With his Jewish wife Drusilla he hears Paul on righteousness, self-control and coming judgment and becomes afraid; he sends Paul away but keeps summoning him, hoping for money, and on leaving office leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.
31587: Antonius Felix, a former slave freed by the imperial family and brother of the powerful freedman Pallas, governed Judea from about 52 to 59. His rule saw rising violence, including the Egyptian false prophet (compare Acts 21:38) and the sicarii assassins. He kept Paul in custody at Caesarea for two years, alternately fascinated and frightened by his preaching and hoping for a bribe.
31588: Acts says he had accurate knowledge of the Way, was married to Drusilla who was Jewish, became frightened at Paul's message about judgment, hoped for money, and left Paul in prison for two years to please the Jews.
31589: His reply, Go away for the present; when I have a convenient season I will call for you (Acts 24:25), is a classic example of procrastination in response to conscience.
31590: Roman historians portray him harshly; the date of his recall is debated (c. 55 vs 59-60) and affects Pauline chronology.
31591: Felix exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave, indulging in every kind of cruelty and lust.
31593: Felix arranged the murder of the former high priest Jonathan by hired assassins.
31595: Smooth, calculating and evasive; speaks politely, delays decisions, and listens for what can be gained.
31599: Earlier accession on the early recall date for Felix
31601: Succeeds Felix and receives the charges
31602: Three days after arriving he goes up to Jerusalem, where the chief priests ask him to transfer Paul there, planning an ambush; he insists they come to Caesarea.
31603: When Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, asks Paul if he will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar; after conferring with his council Festus agrees: to Caesar you shall go.
31605: Unsure what to write to the emperor, he lays the case before Agrippa. During Paul's defense he shouts that Paul's great learning is driving him mad; Paul replies that he speaks true and rational words.
31606: Porcius Festus succeeded Felix as governor of Judea and inherited Paul's unresolved case. Refusing to hand Paul over to a Jerusalem trial where he would face an ambush but willing to compromise, he accepted Paul's appeal to Caesar and, with Agrippa II's help, prepared the case for Rome. He died in office around 62; in the interval before his successor arrived, the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus executed.
31607: Acts portrays him as a correct but politically cautious official who insisted on Roman procedure, wanted to please the Jewish leaders, found the dispute to be about one Jesus who had died whom Paul asserted to be alive (Acts 25:19), and thought Paul mad.
31608: Josephus portrays Festus as a fairly effective governor who suppressed sicarii and a false prophet; the date of his accession is a key point in Pauline chronology and is debated (c. 59-60 is most common).
31609: Festus dealt firmly with brigands and sicarii and with an impostor who promised salvation in the wilderness.
31611: After Festus died, and before Albinus arrived, Ananus convened the Sanhedrin and had James the brother of Jesus stoned.
31613: Brisk, practical and impatient with theology; a Roman administrator who wants a clear charge sheet and finds talk of resurrection baffling.
31619: Seth fathers Enosh at 105. Genesis adds that in Enosh's time people began to call on the name of the LORD.
31621: At 90 he fathers Kenan. He lives 905 years and dies.
31622: Enosh is Seth's son and Adam's grandson. His name is an ordinary Hebrew word for 'human being', often with a sense of weakness or mortality. Genesis ties his lifetime to a new beginning: 'then began men to call upon the name of the LORD'.
31623: Seth fathered Enosh at 105. In his days people began to call on the LORD's name. He fathered Kenan at 90 and died at 905. He appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles and Luke.
31625: The note about calling on the LORD marks the start of public worship among Seth's line, set against the violence of Cain's line in Genesis 4.
31627: Some rabbis read the Hebrew verb as 'profaned' rather than 'began', so that Enosh's generation started idolatry by giving God's name to created things. The Hebrew allows both readings.
31628: Quiet and reverent, a man who feels his own frailty and turns that into prayer.
31631: possibly 'possession' or 'smith'; related to the name Cain
31633: Born to Enosh, he fathers Mahalalel at 70 and lives 910 years.
31634: Kenan is the fourth generation from Adam in Seth's line. Genesis records only his birth, his son and his age. His name sounds like Cain's, and several names in Seth's list echo names in Cain's list (Genesis 4), which scholars have long noticed.
31635: Son of Enosh. He fathered Mahalalel at 70 and lived 910 years. Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him as Cainan.
31636: The similar names in Genesis 4 and 5 (Kenan/Cain, Mahalalel/Mehujael, Jared/Irad, Enoch, Methuselah/Methushael, Lamech) suggest two versions of one ancient name list. This is widely discussed but debated.
31638: They are two separate families. The similar names show the two lines living side by side, one marked by violence and one by worship.
31639: Plain and steady, a man known only for faithfully passing life on.
31645: Born to Kenan, he fathers Jared at 65 and lives 895 years.
31646: Mahalalel, whose name means 'praise of God', is Kenan's son and Jared's father. Genesis gives no story about him, only his place in the line from Adam to Noah.
31647: Son of Kenan. He fathered Jared at 65 and lived 895 years. He appears in 1 Chronicles and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus.
31649: Some preachers read the meanings of the names from Adam to Noah as a hidden sentence about the gospel. This is a popular idea, not a scholarly one, and the meanings it relies on are often uncertain.
31650: Gentle and worshipful, as his name suggests.
31655: At 162 he fathers Enoch, the man who 'walked with God'. Jared lives 962 years, the second-longest life recorded after Methuselah.
31656: Jared is Mahalalel's son and the father of Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. At 962 years his recorded life is second only to his grandson Methuselah's. His name means 'descent', which later Jewish writers connected with a story of angels coming down to earth.
31657: Son of Mahalalel. He fathered Enoch at 162 and lived 962 years in all.
31658: The Book of Watchers says rebel angels came down to earth in the days of Jared, linking his name ('descent') to their fall.
31659: 1 Enoch 6.6 (Jewish apocalyptic text, c. 3rd century BC)
31660: An old, patient elder who has watched many generations come and go.
31664: farmer (implied by his words about the ground)
31666: At 182 he fathers a son and names him Noah, saying this son will bring comfort from the hard toil of working the ground the LORD had cursed.
31668: He lives 777 years. On the Hebrew numbers he dies about five years before the flood.
31669: This Lamech is Methuselah's son and Noah's father. He is a different man from Lamech of Cain's line, who boasted about revenge. This Lamech speaks only once, and his words are a hope: that his son will bring relief from the curse on the ground (Genesis 3:17). That hope connects Noah's story to the first promise of rescue.
31670: Son of Methuselah. At 182 he fathered Noah and said, in effect, 'This one will comfort us in our work and the painful toil of our hands, because of the ground the LORD cursed.' He lived 777 years.
31671: His words show a family that remembered the curse of Genesis 3 and waited for God to answer it. Many see a faint line of hope running from Eve through Lamech to Noah.
31673: The Greek Septuagint gives him 753 years and the Samaritan Pentateuch 653, so the ages in Genesis 5 vary between ancient versions.
31674: When Noah is born with unusual brightness, Lamech fears the child was fathered by an angel, and his father Methuselah goes to Enoch for an answer.
31676: Weary from farming yet hopeful, a man who speaks of comfort and rest.
31682: Shem fathers Arphaxad two years after the flood, when Shem is 100.
31684: At 35 he fathers Shelah and lives another 403 years.
31685: Arphaxad is Shem's son, born two years after the flood. Through him the line of Shem runs on to Eber and, nine generations later, Abraham. Luke's genealogy places an extra name, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah, following the Greek Old Testament.
31686: Son of Shem, born two years after the flood. He fathered Shelah at 35 and lived 403 more years.
31687: The Hebrew text goes straight from Arphaxad to Shelah. The Greek Septuagint and Luke 3:36 have Arphaxad father Cainan, who then fathers Shelah. Scholars debate whether Cainan was added or dropped.
31689: Some link the last part of his name to the Chaldeans (Hebrew Kasdim), but this is uncertain.
31690: A child of the new world after the flood, practical and forward-looking.
31696: At 30 he fathers Eber and lives another 403 years.
31697: Shelah is Arphaxad's son and Eber's father, a link in the chain from Shem to Abraham. He is not the same person as Shelah son of Judah (Genesis 38), who shares the name.
31698: Son of Arphaxad. He fathered Eber at 30 and lived 403 more years. Luke calls him Sala.
31699: A man of few recorded words, remembered as a link in the family line.
31702: the region beyond, the other side
31704: Named as forefather of 'all the children of Eber'
31705: Genesis introduces Shem as 'the father of all the children of Eber', which signals that Eber's line matters.
31707: At 34 he fathers Peleg. His other son, Joktan, becomes the ancestor of Arabian tribes. Eber lives 464 years.
31708: Eber is Shelah's son and the father of Peleg and Joktan. Genesis singles him out: Shem is called 'the father of all the children of Eber'. Many readers connect his name with the word 'Hebrew', the name later given to Abraham (Genesis 14:13). The link is possible but not certain, because 'children of Eber' seems to cover more peoples than Israel alone.
31709: Son of Shelah, father of Peleg and Joktan. He lived 464 years. Balaam's last oracle mentions ships that will 'afflict Eber' (Numbers 24:24).
31710: The Hebrews are named after Eber. Rabbinic stories picture Shem and Eber running a school where later patriarchs studied.
31711: The word 'Hebrew' may come from a root meaning 'cross over', and some compare it with the 'Habiru', landless groups named in Bronze Age texts. The relationship is debated.
31712: A dignified elder, conscious that a people will bear his name.
31716: 'In his days the earth was divided'
31717: Genesis explains his name: in his days the earth was divided. The text does not say what kind of division.
31719: At 30 he fathers Reu and lives another 209 years, 239 in all.
31720: Peleg is Eber's son. His name means 'division', and Genesis says it was given because in his days the earth was divided. Readers have long asked what this means. The most common answer links it to the scattering of peoples and languages at Babel, told in the next chapter.
31721: Son of Eber and brother of Joktan. In his days the earth was divided. He fathered Reu at 30 and lived 239 years.
31723: The 'division' is the scattering of nations at the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1-9).
31724: It refers to dividing land among clans, or to digging irrigation channels, since 'peleg' can mean a water channel (as in Psalm 1:3).
31726: A few suggest it refers to continents splitting apart. Most scholars, including most conservative ones, do not accept this reading.
31727: Thoughtful, a man whose name reminds him that the human family has been broken apart.
31732: At 32 he fathers Serug and lives another 207 years.
31733: Reu is Peleg's son and Serug's father, the sixth generation after Shem. After Peleg, the recorded lifespans in Genesis 11 drop sharply, from over 400 years to around 230. Reu belongs to these shorter-lived generations.
31734: Son of Peleg. He fathered Serug at 32 and lived 239 years in all. Luke calls him Ragau.
31735: Several names in this stretch (Serug, Nahor, Terah, Haran) match place names in northern Mesopotamia near Harran. Some suggest Reu's name may also preserve a regional name, but this is uncertain.
31736: Warm and companionable, as his name suggests.
31741: At 30 he fathers Nahor and lives another 200 years.
31742: Serug is Reu's son and the great-grandfather of Abraham. A town called Sarugi near Harran in northern Mesopotamia is known from Assyrian records, and many scholars think the name of the family and the place are connected.
31743: Son of Reu. He fathered Nahor at 30 and lived 230 years in all. Luke calls him Saruch.
31745: The name matches the town of Sarugi near Harran, which fits Genesis placing Abraham's family in that region.
31746: The Book of Jubilees says that idol worship spread in Serug's day and that he was taught the ways of the Chaldeans.
31748: A man of the northern towns, rooted in the land his descendants would one day leave.
31755: At 29 he fathers Terah, Abraham's father, and lives another 119 years. His 148 years is the shortest recorded life in the list from Shem to Terah.
31756: Nahor son of Serug is Abraham's grandfather. He should not be confused with his grandson Nahor, Abraham's brother, whose family stayed near Harran and produced Rebekah, Laban, Leah and Rachel (Genesis 11:26-29; 24:15). Naming a grandson after a grandfather was a common custom, and the family name probably survives in the 'city of Nahor' (Genesis 24:10).
31757: Son of Serug and father of Terah. He fathered Terah at 29 and lived 148 years in all. Joshua later reminds Israel that their ancestors, including Terah, 'served other gods' beyond the Euphrates.
31758: A town named Nahur near Harran appears in the Mari letters (18th century BC), which supports the idea that the family names reflect real places in northern Mesopotamia.
31759: A head of a Mesopotamian household, at home among the gods of his fathers.
31761: possibly 'we will rebel' (folk etymology); origin debated
31765: The first 'mighty one' on the earth
31766: Cush fathers Nimrod, who 'began to be a mighty one in the earth'. The Hebrew word (gibbor) means a warrior or strongman.
31767: A mighty hunter before the LORD
31768: He becomes proverbial: people say 'Like Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD'.
31770: His kingdom begins with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia).
31772: From there he (or, in the KJV reading, Asshur) goes into Assyria and builds Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah and Resen.
31773: Nimrod is a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham. Genesis calls him the first 'mighty one' on earth and a famous hunter, and credits him with founding the great cities of Babylonia and Assyria. He is the Bible's first picture of a king who builds an empire. Centuries later the prophet Micah calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'. Genesis never says he built the Tower of Babel, but later Jewish writers made that connection, and it became a popular tradition.
31774: Son of Cush. A mighty one and a mighty hunter 'before the LORD'. His kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in Shinar, and he (or Asshur) built Nineveh and other Assyrian cities. Micah 5:6 uses 'the land of Nimrod' for Assyria.
31776: 'Before the LORD' means 'in defiance of the LORD'. Nimrod is the rebel who organised Babel and hunted men as well as animals.
31778: 'Before the LORD' is simply a superlative, meaning 'very great', and Genesis 10 is neutral about him.
31779: He may reflect memories of an early Mesopotamian king or hero. Suggestions include Sargon of Akkad, Tukulti-Ninurta I, or the god Ninurta. None is certain.
31780: Energy, strength and ability to organise
31781: Later tradition sees his empire-building as pride against God
31782: Founding the first kingdom in Shinar
31783: Nimrod persuaded people to build the tower at Babel as an act of defiance against God.
31785: Commanding and proud, a hunter-king who measures everything by strength and conquest.
31790: He marries Adah and Zillah, the first marriage to more than one wife recorded in the Bible.
31792: His sons Jabal, Jubal and Tubal-cain become the fathers of herding, music and metalwork. His daughter is Naamah.
31794: He boasts to his wives that he killed a man for wounding him, and says that if Cain is avenged seven times, Lamech will be avenged seventy-seven times.
31795: This Lamech is a fifth-generation descendant of Cain, through Enoch (Cain's son), Irad, Mehujael and Methushael. He is not Noah's father. He marries two wives, fathers the founders of herding, music and metalwork, and sings a short poem bragging about killing a man. His song shows violence growing worse from Cain onward. Jesus' command to forgive 'seventy times seven' (Matthew 18:22) is often read as a deliberate reversal of Lamech's boast.
31796: Descendant of Cain through Enoch, Irad, Mehujael and Methushael. He married Adah and Zillah. Adah bore Jabal and Jubal; Zillah bore Tubal-cain and Naamah. He boasted that he had killed a man for wounding him and claimed seventy-sevenfold vengeance.
31798: Lamech shows sin spreading and growing: from Cain's murder to boasting about killing. Jesus answers his 'seventy-seven times' revenge with 'seventy times seven' forgiveness.
31799: Genesis 4 shows that culture and technology (cities, music, metal) grew in Cain's line. Skill and wickedness rise together; the text does not condemn the crafts themselves.
31800: Boastful and threatening, a man who sings about revenge.
31807: Born to Lamech and Adah, he is 'the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle'.
31808: Jabal is Lamech's son by Adah. Genesis names him as the father, meaning the founder, of people who live in tents and raise livestock. His full brother Jubal founded music, and his half-brother Tubal-cain founded metalworking.
31809: Son of Lamech and Adah, brother of Jubal. He was the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock.
31810: Genesis 4 explains where the main ways of life came from: herding, music and metalwork. 'Father' here means founder or model, not literal ancestor of all herders.
31811: Practical and outdoors, a herdsman at home with tents and animals.
31818: Forger of bronze and iron tools
31819: Born to Lamech and Zillah, he forges all kinds of tools from bronze and iron. His sister is Naamah.
31820: Tubal-cain is Lamech's son by Zillah. Genesis calls him the one who forged tools of bronze and iron. The second part of his name, 'cain', can mean 'smith', so his name may mean 'Tubal the smith'. He is the Bible's first metalworker.
31821: Son of Lamech and Zillah, brother of Naamah, half-brother of Jabal and Jubal. He forged every kind of tool of bronze and iron.
